clusters.title: You have a higher chance of getting cancer at a younger age than your parents. So what went wrong? | Devi Sridhar
clusters.neutral_headline: You have a higher chance of getting cancer at a younger age than your parents.

items.title: You have a higher chance of getting cancer at a younger age than your parents. So what went wrong? | Devi Sridhar
items.standfirst: Some change in our lifestyles and environments over a generation has caused this increased risk. What, exactly, is a mysteryProf Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghIn the field of global health, we often talk about each generation living longer and healthier lives than their parents. We’ve seen this in the gains in life expectancy, the sharp decrease in child mortality and in the near elimination of many vaccine-preventable diseases. But since the turn of the century this progress has stalled, and in some cases several health metrics have gone backwards.Take cancer, which was long thought to be a disease linked to old age. While most cancers do indeed still occur in elderly people, a new report highlights that a number of cancers are increasing in people who are under 50, often referred to as “early onset cancer”. The report, undertaken by the World Cancer Research Fund, looked at data from 12 different cancer types in England, the US and the Netherlands over the past 20 years. What they found isn’t pretty.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Continue reading...

clusters.title: The Guardian view on cancers in under-50s: the risks of obesity must be confronted | Editorial
clusters.neutral_headline: The Guardian view on cancers in under-50s: the risks of obesity...

items.title: The Guardian view on cancers in under-50s: the risks of obesity must be confronted | Editorial
items.standfirst: More research into the troubling rise in early onset cancers is needed. But we already know that food is among the culpritsThe latest findings about the rise in cancers in people under 50, from the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), are extremely concerning. While a cancer diagnosis is bad news at any time, it is a particular blow for those in younger age groups where most people are in good health. Overlapping trends observed in England, the Netherlands and the US include a troubling rise in the incidence of colorectal (or bowel) cancer. Other diseases that have increased in England include uterine and kidney cancers.These diseases are still rare in young people: 10 times more adults in their 50s, 60s and 70s are diagnosed than those in their 20s, 30s and 40s. Earlier detection is thought to be one factor behind the rise in younger patients. Diagnosing more cancers sooner is an explicit policy goal in England, where late diagnosis and lower uptake of screening are two reasons for mortality rates that are higher than elsewhere in Europe. Continue reading...
